title: Beef Wellington
description:
Beef Wellington, somewhat like, Beef Bourguignon , is a very “important” dish, according to Julia Child, where this recipe came from. We’ve served it for Andrea at Easter, with some of her PSU buddies, and Christmas with friends and family. We’ve never made it, though, on Bastille Day – who would with a name that has Wellington in it – even though it came from Julia’s book, called “Mastering the Art of French Cooking.” (Someday, we may cook our way through the two volumes of her cookbook, but that may take even more time than working on AFOOFT.)
In any case, this is special – the best cut of meat, a tasty stuffing, wonderful fresh breadiness, and all part of a beautiful presentation. Also, much of the labor can be done ahead of time, making the “day-of” preparation a bit easier.
It’s also good, if you have time, to make a luxurious gravy, maybe a little extra to freeze.
START TO FINISH: OVERNIGHT
Beef Wellington
Preheat the oven to 325 degrees.
Heat the butter and/or oil in a large oven-proof pot to moderately hot and brown the meat pieces on all the sides that you can, 5-7 minutes. (This may require a couple of batches.) Remove the meat to a dish.
ingredients: 2-5 pounds meat trimmings, or inexpensive beef pieces, some with bones
directions: Afterwards, strain the solids from the liquid. (If you want a clearer gravy, don’t push down on the vegetables, etc. You can save these vegetable and meat solids, without the bay leaf and thyme, for picking on or another quick soup or sauce with noodles.)

If you have time, after cooling, refrigerate the liquid overnight, allowing you to easily separate the fat the next day (the sauce may be jelly-like from the gelatin in the meat). Otherwise, skim off or separate as much fat as you can.
Add the beef back to the vegetable pot, along with all the broths.
Bring to boil, and with the cover on but slightly ajar, cook in the oven for 3-4 hours.
Pour off any excessive fat and then sauté all the vegetables and herbs over moderate heat, until slightly browned, 5-7 minutes.
Then with the processor going, slowly pour the yeast-egg-milk, watching carefully until the dough balls up on top of the steel blade. (You may need to add a little more flour if it’s too sticky.)
Process for 15 seconds more.
Take dough and let rest for 2 to 3 minutes. Then knead by hand briefly until the dough cleans the butter off the kneading surface and off your hands.
For the first rise, place the dough in a big mixing bowl or pot, cover with plastic wrap, and let rise in a warm place for 3 to 4 hours.
Deflate the risen dough by vigorously punching it. Re-shape it into a smaller ball, cover it again with plastic wrap, and let it rise a second time for 1 ½ to 2 hours in the refrigerator.
Deflate the dough again, cover it with plastic wrap, a plate, and a 5-pound weight (or some kitchen items) so that it will not rise again. Refrigerate.
The Stuffing
1 pound fresh mushrooms
3 tablespoons butter
¼ cup minced shallots
1½ tablespoons flour
1/3 cup dry Madeira
½ cup foie gras, or finely minced
pancetta or bacon
1 egg yolk
½ teaspoon dried tarragon
You can also make this in the morning or the day before. When the meat is stuffed, tied, wrapped in plastic, and refrigerated a day before roasting, it will pick up added flavor.
Dice the trimmed and cleaned mushrooms by hand or in a food processor with several on/off pulses.
Twist a handful at a time in the corner of a towel to extract as much juice as possible.
Heat the butter to foaming in a frying pan, stir in the mushrooms, shallots, and bacon or pancetta pieces if using. Sauté, over moderately high heat, stirring frequently about 5 minutes.
Sprinkle in the flour and stir over moderate heat for 2 minutes.
Remove from heat, blend in the Madeira, and stir again over heat for 1 minute.
Remove from heat, stir in foie gras (if using), the egg yolk, tarragon, and salt and pepper to taste. Set aside.
At this point you should have about 3 quarts of rich liquid. Gently bring this to a boil and simmer until you’ve reduced the sauce to about 2 cups velvety gravy, about 1 hour.
Keep what you need for the meal at hand (you can freeze any extra).

For the final preparation, heat the gravy, check for salt and pepper to taste, and swirl in 2 tablespoons of butter for each cup of sauce. (You could also stir in some finely minced shallots and parsley if you want just a little extra perkiness.)
Bread Crust (Pain Brioche)
3 packages dry-active yeast
¼ cup warm water
1 tablespoon salt
2 tablespoons sugar
¼ cup warm milk
3½ cups all-purpose flour
4 eggs (set in warm water
1 stick butter (¼ pound)

You can make this in the morning or the day before. Also, this will be more bread than you need but it’s better to have some extra, and maybe you can bake the extra for a little croissant for toast and jelly.
Sprinkle the yeast in warm water and let it liquefy completely. Then stir in the salt, sugar, milk, and four beaten eggs.
Measure the flour into a food processor fitted with a steel blade.
Cut butter into pieces and add to the flour.
Process for several seconds until the butter is broken into the flour.
Baste or spray the “sausage” with butter or cooking oil and roast the beef for 25 minutes, basting and turning several times.
Transfer the beef to a platter or tray (reserve the roasting pan) and let the meat cool to room temperature.
If you are pre-roasting a day ahead, cover and refrigerate the meat after it has cooled. Be sure to set the beef at room temperature for 2 hours before the final baking.
Spoon out the fat from the roasting pan, pour in a ½ cup of port wine or Madeira, and boil down by half, scraping up any roasting juices with a wooden spoon. Add this liquid to your gravy.
Trim off any excess dough and reserve it for decorations. Tuck the covering dough against the bottom rectangle of dough and under the bottom of the meat, sealing the edges with your fingers.
Paint the dough covering with an egg glaze (1 egg beaten with a teaspoon of water). After a moment, paint another coat of egg glaze.
For any decorations on the crust, use some dough paste-ons and make some cuts with a sharp knife or scissors.

Immediately after the decorations are complete, set the beef and pan in the oven. The object here is to make sure the dough remains a crust, a thin and crisp covering; if it rises, it will be thick and bready.
Bake in the lower-middle level of the preheated 425-degree oven for 20 to 25 minutes, or until the pastry has browned nicely.

Lower the heat to 350 degrees and cover the crust with foil if it seems to be browning too much. Cook for another 5-10 minutes, when you begin to smell the beef and stuffing and the juices begin to escape into the pan.
Finish up the gravy from the earlier description.

When the meat is done, remove it from the oven and slide it onto a platter or board. The beef will stay warm for 20 minutes; if you still cannot serve it, set in a warming oven no hotter than 120 degrees.
Here you’ll usually have oo’s and ah’s!
To serve, cut all around the crust and an inch or two from its top. Lift the top crust off onto the platter and cut into serving portions.

Separate the slices of meat with a spoon and fork and cut down through the bottom crust so that each slice is served with a portion of stuffing and crust. Spoon a little sauce around the meat and add a piece of the top crust.
A little bit of work – but mainly love!
Preparing the Filet
1 beef tenderloin, trimmed,
8 to 10 inches long and as
even as possible in diame-
ter (2 ½ pounds or more)
½ cup port wine or Madeira
1 egg
cheesecloth
As noted before, this is better to do in the morning or the day before.
With a sharp knife, cut the meat into 16 even slices, about ½ inch thick, keeping them in order.
Lay cheesecloth on a tray and spray with cooking oil.
Salt and pepper each slice, spread with 1 ½ tablespoons or so or stuffing, and reform the roast, arranging the slices against each other on the cheesecloth.
Tie one loop of string around the length of the re-formed roast to hold the slices against each other. Then stretch the cheesecloth tightly over the meat to enclose it.
Twist each end of the cheesecloth closely against each end of the meat; tie securely with the string.

Then twist a spiral of string around the circumference from one end to the other and back again, so that the meat will keep its shape. It will look like a fat sausage about 12 inches long and 4 inches in diameter.
Final Preparation (1 to 1 ½ hours before serving)
Preheat oven to 425 degrees.
Cut the wrapping and string from the beef.

Working somewhat rapidly from now on, so the brioche dough softens as little as possible, roll ¼+ of the dough into a rough long oval, ¼ inch thick and a little longer and wider than the beef. Roll it up on your rolling pin and unroll it onto an oiled pan.
With its most attractive side up, lay the beef on the oval of dough. Trim of the excess dough from around the beef so that there is a ½ inch edge or so.

Take the rest of the dough, roughly twice the size of the initial one used, and roll it into another long oval ¼ inch thick and large enough to enclose the beef (probably about 18 inches long and 8 inches wide). Roll it up on your rolling pin and unroll it over the beef.
